etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English his, from Old English his (“his; its”), from Proto-Germanic *hes (“of this”), genitive of Proto-Germanic *hiz (“this, this one”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe-, *ḱey- (“this”). Cognate with Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, Icelandic hans (“his”). More at he; see also its.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book IIII, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], part II (books IV–VI), London:  […]  [Richard Field] for William Ponsonby, →OCLC, stanza 41:
quote.text: With that he put his ſpurres vnto his ſteed,  With ſpeare in reſt, and toward him did fare,  Like ſhaft out of a bow preuenting ſpeed.

definitions.definition: (archaic) Used as a genitive marker in place of ’s after a noun, especially a masculine noun ending in -s, to express the possessive case. [from 11th c.]
That or those belonging to him; the possessive case of he, used without a following noun.

quote.citation: 2009, John M. Carney, Welcome to Tranquility:
quote.text: The Hikkams pushed a table over by the booth where the Lochwoods and Meekums were sitting, exchanged his and sat down.
